lessons.title: cron: running jobs on a schedule
lessons.goal:
Learn the five time fields of a crontab, install a job, see it run, and learn the traps of cron's minimal environment.

Why it matters: cron has been the standard scheduler for decades. You will read and write crontabs on almost every server.

setup.note: Steps here wait up to a minute (cron and at work in whole minutes). They add and remove a test crontab entry, one `at` job and a few `lab-*` timers.
commands: crontab -r 2>/dev/null; sudo systemctl stop lab-tick.timer lab-tick.service lab-later.timer 2>/dev/null; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/lab-tick.*; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; true

steps.title: The five fields
steps.text:
A crontab line is `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command`.

- `*` any value, `*/5` every 5, `1,15` a list, `9-17` a range.
- `0 3 * * *` every day at 03:00. `*/10 * * * *` every ten minutes. `30 2 * * 1` Mondays at 02:30.
- Shortcuts: `@reboot`, `@hourly`, `@daily`, `@weekly`.

steps.title: Install a job
steps.text: `crontab -` installs the lines it reads as your crontab. Our job runs **every minute**, writes the time and the `PATH` it saw into a file, and nothing else.

run.cmd: echo '* * * * * echo "ran at second $(date +\%S) with PATH=$PATH" >> /tmp/lab/cron.out' | crontab -

steps.after: In a crontab `%` has a special meaning (newline), so it must be written `\%`.

steps.title: Wait for it
steps.text: cron checks once per minute. We wait for the next minute boundary plus a few seconds.
steps.after: The job ran, and its `PATH` is short: `/usr/bin:/bin`. Cron does **not** load your `.bashrc` or profile.

steps.title: The environment trap
steps.text: A job that works in your terminal and fails in cron is almost always an environment difference: the short `PATH`, no `HOME` variables from your profile, a different working directory (your home), and `/bin/sh` instead of bash. Use full paths and set what you need at the top of the crontab (`PATH=...`, `MAILTO=...`).

steps.title: Where the system's jobs live and what cron logs
steps.text: System jobs go in `/etc/cron.d/*` (with an extra user field), or scripts in `/etc/cron.hourly`, `cron.daily`, ... run by `run-parts`. cron logs each start in the journal.

run.cmd: sudo grep 'CMD (echo' /var/log/cron | tail -n 1 | sed -E 's/^.*(\(opc\) CMD)/\1/' | cut -c1-60

steps.under: `crond` reads all crontabs into memory and sleeps until the next minute where a job is due. For each due job it `fork`s, switches to the job's user, sets a minimal environment, and `exec`s `/bin/sh -c COMMAND`. Output is mailed to the user (if a mail system exists) unless redirected, which is why jobs should log to a file or `logger`.

steps.title: Remove the job
steps.text: `crontab -r` removes your whole crontab (no confirmation). `crontab -e` edits it in `$EDITOR`.

quiz.explain: Step value on the minute field.

quiz.q: A script works by hand but fails in cron with `command not found`. Most likely cause?
options: A different, shorter PATH in cron
quiz.explain: Use absolute paths or set PATH.

quiz.q: How do you write `%` in a crontab command?
Where do packages put their system cron jobs?

check.scenario: A nightly backup in cron silently stopped working three weeks ago. How do you find out why and make it visible in future?
check.answer: `journalctl -u crond --since ...` / `/var/log/cron` shows whether it ran; the job's own output is mailed or lost, so redirect it: `... >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1` or use `logger`. Check exit codes, add monitoring (a dead-man's switch such as a healthcheck ping at the end of the job), and consider a systemd timer for logging and alerting.

lessons.title: at and systemd timers
lessons.goal:
Learn one-time jobs with `at`, and systemd timers: transient timers, calendar expressions and a repeating timer.

Why it matters: timers give you logging, dependencies and "run it if the machine was off" behaviour that cron cannot. You will meet both.

setup.note: Steps here wait up to a minute (cron and at work in whole minutes). They add and remove a test crontab entry, one `at` job and a few `lab-*` timers.
commands: crontab -r 2>/dev/null; sudo systemctl stop lab-tick.timer lab-tick.service lab-later.timer 2>/dev/null; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/lab-tick.*; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; true

steps.title: at: run once, later
steps.text: `at TIME` reads commands from stdin and runs them once at that time. `atq` lists the queue. The `atd` service executes the jobs.

run.cmd: echo 'echo "at job ran" > /tmp/lab/at.out' | at now + 1 minute 2>&1 | sed -E 's/ at .*//'
run.output:
warning: commands will be executed using /bin/sh
job 2

steps.title: A one-shot timer with systemd-run
steps.text: `systemd-run --on-active=3s CMD` creates a **transient** timer and service. No unit files are needed.

run.cmd: sudo systemd-run --on-active=3s --unit=lab-later --collect sh -c 'echo ran-later > /tmp/lab/later.out' 2>&1 | sed 's/^Running timer as unit: /timer: /; s/^Will run service as unit: /service: /'

steps.title: Calendar expressions
steps.text: `OnCalendar=` uses a readable syntax: `DayOfWeek Year-Month-Day Hour:Minute:Second`. `systemd-analyze calendar` shows the **normalized** form and the next runs, so you can test before deploying.

run.cmd: systemd-analyze calendar 'Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00' --iterations=2 | grep -E 'Normalized|Next elapse|Iteration' | sed -E 's/\(.*\)//; s/ +/ /g'
run.output:
Normalized form: Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00:00
 Next elapse: Mon 2026-11-09 09:00:00 GMT

run.cmd: systemd-analyze calendar daily | grep Normalized | sed 's/ +/ /g'

steps.title: A repeating timer: two unit files
steps.text: A timer unit triggers a service unit with the same name. This one runs `lab-tick.service` one second after activation and then **every 2 seconds**. The job is `Type=oneshot`.

code.src:
[Unit]
Description=Lab tick timer

[Timer]
OnActiveSec=1s
OnUnitActiveSec=2s
AccuracySec=100ms

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

steps.after: `OnActiveSec` counts from the moment the timer is started; `OnUnitActiveSec` counts from the last time the service was activated. Save the second file, shown next, as `lab-tick.service`: it is the job the timer starts.

steps.title: The service unit, run, and the log
steps.text: Install both, start the timer for 7 seconds, and count the runs. Each run is a normal service run, so its status is in the journal.

code.src:
[Unit]
Description=Lab tick job

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo "tick at $(date +%S)" >> /tmp/lab/tick.log'

run.cmd: sudo cp lab-tick.timer lab-tick.service /etc/systemd/system/; sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start lab-tick.timer; sleep 7; sudo systemctl stop lab-tick.timer; wc -l < /tmp/lab/tick.log | awk '{print $1, "ticks in about 7 seconds"}'
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/lab-tick.timer /etc/systemd/system/lab-tick.service; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; echo cleaned

steps.under: A timer can be **monotonic** (`OnBootSec=`, `OnActiveSec=`, `OnUnitActiveSec=`: relative to an event) or **realtime** (`OnCalendar=`: wall clock). `Persistent=true` runs a missed calendar job at the next boot. `RandomizedDelaySec=` spreads load. `systemctl list-timers` shows the next and last run of every timer.

quiz.q: What starts a command once at a future time?
Which timer setting runs a missed calendar job after the machine was off?
quiz.explain: Persistent=true stores the last run time.

options: Shows the normalized form and the next elapse times
quiz.explain: It lets you test an OnCalendar expression.

quiz.q: A timer unit `X.timer` starts which unit by default?
quiz.explain: The service with the same name.

check.scenario: Compare cron and systemd timers for a nightly report, and say when you would pick each.
check.answer: Timers: journal logging and exit status per run, dependencies and sandboxing from the service unit, `Persistent=` for missed runs, randomized delay, no mail surprises, `systemctl list-timers`. Cron: simple, universal, one line, works on any Unix. Pick timers on systemd hosts for anything important or long-running; cron for quick personal jobs and portability.

interview.q: Write a crontab line for 02:30 every Monday.
interview.a: `30 2 * * 1 /path/to/command`. Fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. See [the lesson](#/lesson/27/cron).

interview.q: Why does a job work in the shell but not in cron?
interview.a: Cron's environment is minimal (short PATH, no profile, different shell and working directory). Use absolute paths and set variables in the crontab.

interview.q: How do you run a command once, in two hours?
interview.a: `echo 'cmd' | at now + 2 hours` (check with `atq`, remove with `atrm`), or `systemd-run --on-active=2h cmd`.

interview.q: What are the advantages of systemd timers over cron?
interview.a: Logging through the journal, per-run status, dependencies, resource limits and sandboxing, Persistent= for missed runs, randomized delay, easy manual start. See [the lesson](#/lesson/27/at-and-timers).

interview.q: How do you test an OnCalendar expression?
interview.a: `systemd-analyze calendar 'EXPR' --iterations=5` prints the normalized form and the next run times.
Running daily/weekly/monthly jobs on machines that are not always on: it runs missed jobs after boot, using timestamps. systemd's Persistent=true does the same.

glossary.def: The traditional scheduler that runs commands at times defined in crontabs.
A file with schedule lines for cron, one per user or in /etc/cron.d.
Runs a command once at a given time.
A systemd unit that starts a service on a schedule or after an event.
Timer setting with a wall-clock schedule expression.
A unit created at run time by systemd-run, without a unit file.
